title: The third paragraph (Numbers 15:37–41)
hook: the fringes, and the Exodus remembered morning and night

segments.voice: Yesterday, avodah shebalev and the second paragraph, rain and harvest tied to what a community does. Your line was what we do matters. Which action did you do well anyway? Today, the Shema's last paragraph. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

People tie strings around fingers. They write on the backs of their hands. They set a photo as the lock screen, wear a ring, keep a stone from a beach in their pocket. Humans are forgetful, and we know it, so we hang reminders on our bodies. The third paragraph of the Shema is about exactly that: a reminder you wear. And in many synagogues, while it's being read, you'll see people lift the fringes they gathered earlier and kiss them, again and again, at one particular word.
screen: `A STRING AROUND A FINGER.` → `REMINDERS WE WEAR.` → `KISSING THE FRINGES.`

segments.voice: The paragraph comes from the Book of Numbers. God tells Moses to have the people make tzitzit, fringes, on the corners of their garments, with a thread of blue in each. And the reason is given right there. In the old Jewish translation: "that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them." Look, remember, do. And then a warning: not to go wandering after your own heart and your own eyes. The eyes see things and the heart wants them; the fringes are a counterweight you can see. The word tzitzit appears three times in the paragraph, and many people kiss the fringes at each one. The blue thread, tekhelet, came from a dye whose source was lost for many centuries; some people today wear blue threads again from a dye they believe is the ancient one, while others wear all white. Then the paragraph ends with the Exodus: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. That's why this paragraph is said at night, too, even though fringes are a daytime commandment. The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, records an old argument: must the Exodus be remembered at night? Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah says he couldn't win the point until Ben Zoma read a verse: all the days of your life. The days of your life means the days. All the days includes the nights. So the Exodus is remembered twice a day, morning and evening, every day.
screen: `TZITZIT ON THE CORNERS.` · `LOOK, REMEMBER, DO.` · `NOT AFTER YOUR HEART AND EYES.` · `ALL THE DAYS INCLUDES THE NIGHTS.` · then, large: `REMEMBER TWICE A DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: kiss something meaningful. Settle, and breathe. Look around you, or in your pocket, or on your hand, for an object that carries a memory: a ring, a photo, a book someone gave you, a scarf, a child's drawing. Pick it up. Look at it, and let it remind you of what it stands for. Who gave it. What it asks of you. Then, if it feels right, kiss it, or press it to your heart, the way people kiss the fringes. Look, remember, do. The bell holds the time.
Tzitzit. Fringes, tied to the four corners of a garment — look at them, the Torah says, and remember all the commandments, and do them.
Your line: remember twice a day. Today, look at your reminder once in the morning and once at night, and remember what it's for. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: The third paragraph of the Shema, Numbers 15:37–41, is said morning and evening; in the morning, many people holding their tzitzit kiss them each time the word is said and look at them while reading.

what a scholar hears: Numbers 15:37–41; Mishnah Berakhot 1:5 (Elazar ben Azariah and Ben Zoma on Deuteronomy 16:3); Menachot 43b on tzitzit; the modern recovery of tekhelet is debated.

notes: Numbers 15:39 phrase quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.
Mishnah Berakhot 1:5: Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah ('I am like seventy years old') and Ben Zoma's reading of Deuteronomy 16:3; confirm.
The word tzitzit appears three times in the paragraph (15:38 twice, 15:39 once); confirm count and the kissing custom.
Tekhelet: dye source (chilazon) lost; modern identification with Murex trunculus accepted by some, not others. Presented neutrally; confirm.
Third paragraph recited at night for the Exodus though tzitzit are not obligatory at night; confirm.
